PROJECT DESCRIPTION
     305 Beacon hotel operations summary.

This proposed hotel, located at 305 Beacon Street, is
comprised of 9 hotel rooms and one employee housing
unit. Amenities include a roof top deck and adult
swimming pool.

This hotel will operate in concert with the recently
approved 301 Beacon hotel, known as “ The Cameron
Hotel”. These two facilities are owned by two long time
families of Avalon whom wish to maintain separate land
ownerships but with a common lease eﬀort for 50 years.
will appear as one operating hotel.
Design has considered the separate ownership by
maintaining separate building structures and
infrastructure while utilizing one lobby. Carefull
consideration has been worked into the design so in the
event 5 decades from now, 301 and 305 could easily be
separated and operate as two separate hotels
This combined hotel opportunity allows for eﬃcient 24
hour on sight management, eﬃcient housekeeping and
guest services by sharing onsite employees which will
have the opportunity to live onsite in new housing
facilities. The approved 301 Beacon hotel includes a
lobby for check in and check out, gym facility, laundry
facilities, roof top lounge area and intends to share these
amenities with the patrons of the proposed 305 Beacon
 hotel. The amenities of 305 Beacon including roof top
deck and swimming pool will also provide access to the
Patrons of 301 Beacon.

The roof top decks each will have separate elevators and
can share secondary emergency access with each other.
 Operational Phasing of 305 Beacon Street Hotel

305 Beacon Street Hotel is proposed to be completely
constructed at one time by March of 2027.

This proposed hotel has 3 existing water credits because
there are 3 bedrooms and a operational water meter for
the existing structure which can be transferred to the new
project. Upon completion of construction there will be one
employee housing unit and 9 new hotel units. The seven
remaining rooms will require a water allocation upon their
completion. Currently this project is on the Southern
California Edison water allocation waiting list. It is
anticipated based on Edison’s forecasting that
additional water will be available in the third quarter of
2026. This proposed project anticipates to open for
business in March of 2027. However in the event that the
hotel is ready to open but the water has still not been
released, the seven rooms will not be occupied until either
the applicant has secured the required water allocations.
The employee housing unit will not be part of the initial 3
rooms which are able to be occupied initially. Until all 10
rooms are released there will not a need for any additional
employees.

It is anticipated that the proposed 305 Beacon project will
work in concert with the previously approved phasing
plan for the 301 Beacon Street project.

sprinklers, flooring, fixtures, all furnishings. The

  2  PROJECT OVERVIEW

2.1  Introduction

Pursuant to Section 15367 of the State CEQA Guidelines, the City of Avalon (City) is the public agency that
has the principal responsibility for conducting or approving a project.

Christopherhill Development proposes to demolish the existing, vacant 1,258 SF single-story residential
building on APN 7480-031-041, which is a 2,375 SF lot at 305 Beacon Street near the southeast corner of
Beacon Street and Metropole Avenue, and construct a new 3,811 SF, two-story 9-room hotel with 1
workforce housing unit. The existing building to be demolished is 14 feet high and contains one, three-
bedroom, two-bathroom unit. The Proposed Project would be 26 feet high (from the highest point on the
lot which is located at the rear of the lot) and would contain 9 hotel rooms and one workforce housing
unit, an elevator that would access all floors including the roof, and a rooftop deck that will contain a 492
SF swimming pool and a 68 SF bathroom. At the rooftop, the elevator would extend approximately 10 to
12 feet above the parapet, and the bathroom would extend approximately 4 to 5 feet above the parapet.

Demolition of the existing building would occur with labor and hand power tools, and no heavy equipment
would be utilized except to prepare the building pad for final grading once the building demolition has
been completed. Interior room completion would be completed in one phase, based on water allocations
by Southern California Edison which dictates development in the City based its operation of the City’s
water system. Operations consist of typical hotel operations. The Project Site is zoned as Special
Commercial (SC).

The City, as the lead agency for the Proposed Project, is responsible for preparing environmental
documentation in accordance with CEQA to determine if approval of the discretionary actions requested
and subsequent development of the Proposed Project would have a significant impact on the
environment. As such, this document is designed to meet the requirements for the City of Avalon’s
Environmental Assessment/CEQA compliance.

2.2  Background

Hamilton Pacific, LLC (HP), which is a sister company to the Applicant Christopherhill Development, offers
full service general contracting services throughout Southern California. HP is also currently the developer
and contractor for the Hamilton Cove Development in Avalon, and currently has approximately 15 to 30
construction employees working on any given day depending on the work activity. HP currently houses
employees during the week in a combination of hotels and other transient housing. In November 2024,
the City approved the Applicant’s proposal (Cameron Hotel, PC #2842), to develop a 35-room, four-story,
11,230 SF hotel at 301 Beacon Street located on the adjacent parcel west of the Proposed Project, AIN
7480-031-040. Adjacent to 301 Beacon Street is a single story residential building, 305 Beacon Street, that
has been vacant for more than 30 years and is in a state of disrepair.

2.3  Project Setting and Location

The proposed Project is located just east of the southeast corner of Beacon Street and Metropole Avenue
in the City of Avalon and is identified as 305 Beacon Street, Los Angeles County Assessor Identification No.
(AIN) 7480-031-041. Refer to Figure 1: Regional Vicinity and Figure 2: Project Location located at the end
of this section.

The Project site is within the USGS 7.5’ quadrangle Santa Catalina East, within Topographic Quad
Coordinates: Township 9 South, Range 14 West, Latitude: 33.342598°N / Longitude: -118.328184°W.

2.3.1  Existing Conditions

The Project Site is a vacant 1,258 SF single-story, 14-foot-high single family residence that contains three-
bedrooms and two-bathrooms. The existing building footprint occupies approximately 1,258 SF of the
2,375 SF lot, with an approximately 200 SF patio, and is set back approximately 33 feet from the rear
property line.

The single-story building was constructed in 1940, with no distinctive architectural elements, and no off-
site parking availability. Because the lot slopes from south (higher) to north (lower), as well as from west
(higher) to east (lower), a portion of the unit is constructed below grade, which allows the roofline to
remain flat, similar to the buildings in the immediate vicinity. The existing building is 14 feet high on the
rear of the property, which is highest point on the property. The entrance to the building is through a
walkway on the west side.

The site is completely urbanized, containing no trees or shrubs or other habitat for migratory or special
status species.

The existing building housed once housed the family members of the property owner, but they have not
occupied the building since approximately 1990, and the building is used for the owner’s family’s storage.
As such, the building has fallen into a state of disrepair. The building does not meet current building code
standards.

2.3.3  Topography and Soils

The topography in the vicinity of Metropole Avenue slopes steeply southeasterly to northeasterly from
Tremont Street (south, higher elevation) toward Beacon Street (north, lower elevation). Beacon Street
slopes northwesterly from Calle Del Sol (northwest, higher elevation) to southeasterly (Sumner Avenue,
lower elevation). Therefore, there are elevational changes throughout the Project Site.

The soil series is described by the Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) as urban land-
xerorthents, landscaped, association 0 to 8 percent slopes.

2.3.4  Site Zoning and Approvals

The Project Site is zoned by the City of Avalon as Special Commercial (SC). City of Avalon Code Section 9-
6 identifies that the SC zoning district is provide an area in which both small scale residents and
neighborhood retail and services can coexist harmoniously. The SC area is defined by commercial areas
easterly of Catalina Avenue (between Beacon Street and Third Street); south side of Beacon (Catalina
Avenue to Calle del Sol); and west side of Metropole (Beacon northerly). The SC zoning district is
consistent with the Commercial land use designation of the City’s 2030 General Plan/Local Coastal Plan.

The Project Site is not within any airport zone.

A hotel is permitted within the SC zone with the approval of a Conditional Use Permit (Section 9-6.303).
The Applicant received approval to construct the Cameron Hotel at 301 Beacon Street, from the City of
Avalon through the Planning Commission Application No. 2842 to allow for a new hotel to be constructed
at 301 Beacon.

The Proposed Project would be a new hotel located at 305 Beacon Street, adjacent to the newly-approved
hotel at 301 Beacon Street. The official main entrance to the proposed hotel at 305 Beacon Street would
be through the lobby of the adjacent hotel at 301 Beacon Street, and then through a shared entrance in
the east portion of the lobby of 301 Beacon Street that would lead to a hallway on the west side of the
305 Beacon Street hotel. A door is planned on Beacon Street as a dedicated, secured ingress/egress for
305 Beacon Street. A series of stairs would also connect the rooftop of 305 with the rooftop of 301 Beacon
Street, however, the stairs would be limited only to hotel staff. Each of the hotels will have independent
elevator access. As the Applicant is leasing each of the parcels from the same landowner, each of the
hotels are designed as separate buildings and separate entitlement applications because the landowner
did not want to merge the two parcels to become one hotel. Design plans are contained in Appendix A -
Architectural Plans.

  3  REGULATORY SUMMARY

The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) is codified in Title 14 of the California Code of Regulations
(14 CCR). This statute requires state and local agencies to identify the significant environmental impacts
of their actions and to avoid or mitigate those impacts, if feasible. Guidelines for implementation of the
statute are the regulations that explain and interpret the law for both the public agencies required to
administer CEQA and for the public. They are found in the California Code of Regulations, in Chapter 3 of
Title 14 “Guidelines for Implementation of the California Environmental Quality Act” (Guidelines).

Definition of a Project. Guidelines Section 15378 defines a Project as “the whole of an action, which has
a potential for resulting in either a direct physical change in the environment, or a reasonably foreseeable
indirect physical change in the environment, and that is any of the following:

  (1) An activity directly undertaken by any public agency including but not limited to public works construction
  and related activities clearing or grading of land, improvements to existing public structures, enactment and
  amendment of zoning ordinances, and the adoption and amendment of local General Plans or elements thereof
  pursuant to Government Code Sections 65100-65700.

  (2) An activity undertaken by a person which is supported in whole or in part through public agency contracts,
  grants, subsidies, loans, or other forms of assistance from one or more public agencies.

  (3) An activity involving the issuance to a person of a lease, permit, license, certificate, or other entitlement for
  use by one or more public agencies.

The proposed action is to approve the Project identified as 305 Beacon Street Hotel, an application by
Christopherhill Development for the demolition of an existing single-story residential building and
construction of a 10-room hotel, which qualifies as a Project under the CEQA Guidelines because the
Projects the Project must be approved by a discretionary action by the City of Avalon, Planning
Commission Application No. 2887.

Exemption Review. CEQA Section 15061 (a) states that once a lead agency determines that the activity
is a project under CEQA, the lead agency shall determine if the Project is exempt from CEQA. A Project is
exempt from CEQA if the following apply (Section 15061[b]):

  1) The project is exempt by statute (see, e.g. Article 18, commencing with Section 15260).

  2) The project is exempt pursuant to a categorical exemption (see Article 19, commencing with Section
  15300) and the application of that categorical exemption is not barred by one of the exceptions set
  forth in Section 15300.2.

  3) The activity is covered by the common sense exemption that CEQA applies only to projects which have
  the potential for causing a significant effect on the environment. Where it can be seen with certainty
  that there is no possibility that the activity in question may have a significant effect on the environment,
  the activity is not subject to CEQA.

CEQA Guidelines Article 19, commencing with Section 15300 through Section 15333 identifies 33 classes
of projects that do not have a significant effect on the environment; as such, they are declared to be
categorically exempt from the requirement for the preparation of environmental documents.

Based on the Exemption Review conducted for the Project consistent with CEQA Section 15061 (a), the
Project could be consistent with a Categorical Exemption pursuant to Article 19, commencing with Section
15300. Specifically, the elements of Project identified as a removing an existing single-story structure and
replacing it with a new multi-story structure of similar footprint could qualify under Guidelines Section
15332, Class 32 “In-fill Development Projects.” This class of projects is located in an urban area, generally
consistent with the City’s zoning codes, is less than 5 acres, and where the site has no habitat value for
endangered, rare or threatened species, and can be serviced by existing utilities.

Exceptions to Exemptions. Guidelines Section 15300.2 also identifies exceptions in which a project that
has been deemed to be consistent with Article 19, commencing with Section 15300 through Section 15333
would be barred under the exemption class. These exceptions include 1:

  (a) Location. Classes 3, 4, 5, 6, and 11 are qualified by consideration of where the project is to be located -- a
  project that is ordinarily insignificant in its impact on the environment may in a particularly sensitive
  environment be significant. Therefore, these classes are considered to apply all instances, except where the
  project may impact on an environmental resource of hazardous or critical concern where designated, precisely
  mapped, and officially adopted pursuant to law by federal, state, or local agencies.

  (b) Cumulative Impact. All exemptions for these classes are inapplicable when the cumulative impact of
  successive projects of the same type in the same place, over time is significant.

  (c) Significant Effect. A categorical exemption shall not be used for an activity where there is a reasonable
  possibility that the activity will have a significant effect on the environment due to unusual circumstances.

  (d) Scenic Highways. A categorical exemption shall not be used for a project which may result in damage to
  scenic resources, including but not limited to, trees, historic buildings, rock outcroppings, or similar resources,
  within a highway officially designated as a state scenic highway. This does not apply to improvements which
  are required as mitigation by an adopted negative declaration or certified EIR.

  (e) Hazardous Waste Sites. A categorical exemption shall not be used for a project located on a site which is
  included on any list compiled pursuant to Section 65962.5 of the Government Code.

  (f) Historical Resources. A categorical exemption shall not be used for a project which may cause a substantial
  adverse change in the significance of a historical resource.

  TRAFFIC

  The Project is a 10-room hotel. There would be one golf cart provided for use by the hotel staff.

  at the curb adjacent to the 301 Beacon Street hotel entrance; Beacon Street is approximately 34 feet

  hotels in one trip.

  Standard Trip Generation Estimate

  The Project’s potential trip generation was calculated based on the Transportation Engineers’ (ITE)
  Trip Generation (11th Edition) for a Motel. The ITE Motel use is defined as a place of lodging that
  provides sleeping accommodations and often a restaurant. They generally offer free on-site parking
  and provide little or no meeting space and few (if any) supporting facilities. The Proposed Project does
  not offer parking or meeting spaces.

  It should be noted that the Project is proposed as an “in-fill” in an environment that has access to
  transit and pedestrian convenience and that the existing building was at one time used for permanent
  and transient housing. And though access to the Proposed hotel will be 100 percent from transit and
  pedestrian usage, the ITE Motel classification assumes 100 percent car trips to the site and does not
  account for projects that are 100 percent reliant on other modes of transportation.

  Trip Reduction Calculation Due to Transportation Mode

  Due to the growing number of urban in-fill projects where other modes of transportation could be
  used, the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) in 2009, commissioned a study of travel
  characteristics of in-fill development in California’s metropolitan areas (Study). 2 The Study noted that
  during local land use review and development permitting processes, public agencies commonly
  require estimates of vehicle travel impacts associated with proposed land use projects, assessments
  of their potential contribution to traffic congestion, and identification of appropriate mitigation
  strategies. These strategies often include mitigation fees, private developer contributions, special tax
  assessment districts, and specific infrastructure improvements.

  In preparing traffic and transportation impact analyses, professionals often rely on the ITE published
  trip-generation rates for various types of land uses. However, ITE data typically reflects isolated
  suburban development usually lacking availability and proximity of transit service, and the ITE study
  sites are located such that they are difficult to access by walking or bicycling. The Study indicated that
  the use of ITE trip-generation rates for proposed urban in-fill development projects served by transit
  and having good pedestrian access could significantly over- predict vehicular traffic impacts. The Study
  evaluated various land uses, such as high-rise apartments, retail, office, and several restaurant types.

  A hotel/motel was not among the land uses studied. However, the result of the Study was that for all
  land uses studied, the ITE calculation rate was an average of 35 percent higher in the AM and 26
  percent higher in the PM than what was actually observed.

  Study Methodology

  Three 15-minute ambient noise measurements were conducted on May 1, 2024, as part of the noise
  analysis for the approval of the 301 Beacon Street hotel. The sound level meter measured the Leq,
  Lmin, Lmax, and other statistical data (e.g., L2, L8…). The noise measurements were taken to
  determine the existing ambient noise levels. Noise data indicates that traffic is the primary source of
  noise impacting the site and the adjacent uses. This assessment utilizes the ambient noise data as a
  basis and compares project operational levels to said data.

  The Project’s potential noise was modeled using SoundPLAN (SP) acoustical modeling software that is
  capable of evaluating multiple stationary noise source impacts at various receiver locations. SP’s
  software utilizes algorithms (based on the inverse square law and reference equipment noise level
  data) to calculate noise level projections. The software allows the user to input specific noise sources,
  spectral content, sound barriers, building placement, topography, and sensitive receptor locations.

  Construction Noise

  and construction. However, construction is required to comply with the City’s Municipal Code Section
  5-13.06 which prohibits construction within 500 feet of residential zones, hotels, or motels between
  the hours of 7:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m. or at any time on Sundays.

  As such, there would be a less than significant impact from construction noise.

  5  CATEGORICAL EXEMPTION EXCEPTIONS ANALYSIS

As previously discussed, Guidelines Section 15300.2 also identifies exceptions in which a project that has
been deemed to be consistent with a class of projects may not have an impact on the environment but
would not qualify under the exemption class under certain criteria. The criteria as outlined in Guidelines
Section 15300.2 are provided in italicized type, and the consistency evaluation response is provided in
standard type.

(a) Location. Classes 3, 4, 5, 6, and 11 are qualified by consideration of where the project is to be located -
- a project that is ordinarily insignificant in its impact on the environment may in a particularly sensitive
environment be significant. Therefore, these classes are considered to apply all instances, except where
the project may impact on an environmental resource of hazardous or critical concern where designated,
precisely mapped, and officially adopted pursuant to law by federal, state, or local agencies.

  Discussion. The Project qualifies as Class 32. Therefore, this exception criterion is not applicable.

(b) Cumulative Impact. All exemptions for these classes are inapplicable when the cumulative impact of
successive projects of the same type in the same place, over time is significant.

  Discussion. The City of Avalon is a small community, mostly built out. Construction of various
  smaller projects are on-going throughout the City. The hotel at 301 Beacon Street would be
  constructed at the same time as the Proposed Project at 305 Beacon Street. However, the Project
  construction is required to follow all appliable regulations. Once constructed, the Project would
  be operated in conjunction with 301 Beacon Street. Therefore, Project construction and
  operations are anticipated to create a less than significant cumulative impact.

(c) Significant Effect. A categorical exemption shall not be used for an activity where there is a reasonable
possibility that the activity will have a significant effect on the environment due to unusual circumstances.

  Discussion. The Project would demolish an existing building that has been deemed not
  structurally sound. The demolition would be conducted primarily with hand tools and limited
  power equipment, as well as required to comply with all laws. Standard construction methods
  would be used. There are no unusual circumstances associated with this Project.

(d) Scenic Highways. A categorical exemption shall not be used for a project which may result in damage
to scenic resources, including but not limited to, trees, historic buildings, rock outcroppings, or similar
resources, within a highway officially designated as a state scenic highway. This does not apply to
improvements which are required as mitigation by an adopted negative declaration or certified EIR.

  Discussion. There are no scenic highways with resources, including but not limited to, trees,
  historic buildings, rock outcroppings, or similar resources, within a highway officially designated
  as a state scenic highway located along the Project site. Therefore, there would be no impact.

(e) Hazardous Waste Sites. A categorical exemption shall not be used for a project located on a site which
is included on any list compiled pursuant to Section 65962.5 of the Government Code.

  Discussion. Section 65962.5(a)(1) requires that Department of Toxic Substance Control (DTSC) “shall
  compile and update as appropriate, but at least annually, and shall submit to the Secretary for

305 Beacon Street Hotel - Planning Commission Application No. 2887

  Environmental Protection, a list of all the following: ....(1) [a]ll hazardous waste facilities subject to
  corrective action pursuant to Section 25187.5 of the Health and Safety Code (“HSC”).” The
  hazardous waste facilities identified in HSC § 25187.5 are those where DTSC has taken or contracted
  for corrective action because a facility owner/operator has failed to comply with a date for taking
  corrective action in an order issued under HSC § 25187, or because DTSC determined that immediate
  corrective action was necessary to abate an imminent or substantial endangerment. This is known
  as the “Cortese List.” This is a very small and specific subgroup of facilities and they are not separately
  posted on the DTSC or Cal/EPA’s website. The following databases that meet the “Cortese List”
  requirements were reviewed for this Project.

  Envirostore Database. HSC § 25356(b)(1) requires “a listing of hazardous substance release sites
  selected for, and subject to, a response action under this chapter.” HSC § 25356(b)(2) requires
  DTSC to “update the list of sites at least annually to reflect new information regarding previously
  listed sites or the addition of new sites requiring response action.” The implementing regulations
  provide that sites may be listed pursuant to HSC § 25356 if (a) they are not owned by the Federal
  Government and (b) a release or threatened release of hazardous substances has been confirmed
  by on-site sampling. (California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Section 67400.1). DTSC’s list of sites
  that meet those criteria as well as the criteria in HSC § 25356(c), is found in a report in DTSC’s
  “Envirostor” database. There are no sites listed on the EnviroStore database within the Project
  area.

  Geotracker Database. Geotracker is the SWRCB’s database that manages potential hazardous
  sites to groundwater. There are no sites identified on the Project Site, or adjacent to the Project
  Site. Therefore, the Project would not be located on any site that has been identified in
  accordance with Section 65962.5 of the Government Code.

Therefore, the Project is not located on a site which is included on any list compiled pursuant to Section
65962.5 of the Government Code, nor is there any indication of hazardous waste.

(f) Historical Resources. A categorical exemption shall not be used for a project which may cause a
substantial  adverse  change  in  the  significance  of  a  historical  resource.

  Discussion. Section 15064.5(a) of the CEQA Guidelines defines historical resources, which
  includes: A resource listed in, or determined to be eligible by the State Historical Resources
  Commission, for listing in the California Register of Historical Resources (Pub. Res. Code § 5024.1,
  Title 14 CCR, Section 4850 et seq.).

  Public Resources Code Section 5020.1(q) defines “Substantial adverse change” as the demolition,
  destruction, relocation, or alteration such that the significance of an historical resource would be
  impaired. CEQA Guidelines Section15064.5 (b)(1) and (b)(2) clarify that the impairment must be
  material and states that material impairment of a historical resource would occur when the
  Project “demolishes or materially alters in an adverse manner those physical characteristics of an
  historical resource that convey its historical significance and that justify its inclusion in, or
  eligibility for, inclusion in the California Register of Historical Resources.”

  The existing single-story structure would be demolished. The structure is not identified on the
  State or federal registers for historical resources, nor is it identified in the City’s General Plan EIR

  not cause a substantial adverse change in the significance of a historical resource because there
  are no historical resources on site.

site has no habitat for endangered, rare or threatened species; approval of the Project would not result
in significant effects relating to traffic, noise, air quality, or water quality; and the Project Site and can be
serviced by existing utilities. I have evaluated the criteria for the exceptions to the exemptions as
identified in Guidelines Section 14 CCR, Chapter 3, Article 19, Section 15300.2 and found that there are
no exceptions to the use of an exemption for the Project. Therefore, no further analysis is required. A
Notice of Exemption will be filed with the County of Los Angeles Clerk of the Board.

Subject:  305 Beacon Street Hotel – Cat32 Exemption Noise Impact Assessment – Avalon, CA

Dear Ms. Gilbert:

MD Acoustics, LLC (MD) has completed a noise impact assessment for the proposed hotel project located
at 305 Beacon Street in the City of Avalon, CA. The project has filed for a Categorical 32 Exemption (Cat32),
which is an “Infill” Categorical Exemption (CEQA Guideline Section 15332) that exempts infill development
within urbanized areas if it meets certain criteria. The class consists of environmentally benign infill projects
that are consistent with the local General Plan and Zoning requirements. This class is not intended for
projects that would result in any significant traffic, noise, air quality, or water quality impacts. It may apply
to residential, commercial, industrial, and/or mixed-use projects.

This noise assessment intends to demonstrate the project’s compliance with applicable noise regulations
and lack of significant noise impacts. A list of definitions and terminology is located in Appendix A.

1.0  Project Description and Assessment Overview
The project site is located at 305 Beacon Street within the City of Avalon, California, as shown in Exhibit A.
The site is currently zoned as Special Commercial. Land zoning surrounding the site includes Special
Commercial to the north, south, southeast, and west, and Commercial to the northeast. Metropole Avenue
is to the northwest, and Beacon Street is to the northeast. The Catalina Airport is located approximately 6
miles northwest of the project site.

The project proposes a two (2) story hotel with multiple uses consisting of 10 hotel rooms and a rooftop
deck for guests. The rooftop deck will include a restroom and a shallow adult-only swimming pool and is
assumed to have a maximum capacity of approximately 25 people. The rooftop operational hours will be 8
AM to 10 PM for events and rooftop amenities. See Appendix B for the architectural plans.

2.0  Fundamentals of Noise
The following provides basic information about noise and presents some of the terms used within the
report.

2.1  Human Response to Changes in Noise Levels
In general, the healthy human ear is most sensitive to sounds between 1,000 Hz and 5,000 Hz (A-
weighted scale), and it perceives a sound within that range as being more intense than a sound with a
higher or lower frequency with the same magnitude. For purposes of this report, as well as with most
environmental documents, the A-scale weighting is typically reported in terms of A-weighted decibels
(dBA). Typically, the human ear can barely perceive a change in noise level of 3 dB. A change in 5 dB is
readily perceptible, and a change in 10 dB is perceived as being twice or half as loud. As previously
discussed, a doubling of sound energy results in a 3 dB increase in sound, which means that a doubling
of sound energy (e.g., doubling the volume of traffic on a highway) would result in a barely perceptible
change in sound level.

Noise in our daily environment fluctuates over time. Some noise levels occur in regular patterns, while
others are random. Some noise levels are constant, while others are sporadic. Noise descriptors were
created to describe the different time-varying noise levels.

the A-weighted filter network. The A-weighting filter de-emphasizes the very low and very high-frequency
components of the sound in a manner similar to the response of the human ear. A numerical method of
rating human judgment of loudness.

Ambient Noise Level: The composite of noise from all sources, near and far. In this context, the ambient
noise level constitutes the normal or existing level of environmental noise at a given location.

hour day, obtained after the addition of five (5) decibels to sound levels in the evening from 7:00 to 10:00

receptor locations.

4.5  Construction Vibration Model
Construction activities can produce vibration that may be felt by adjacent land uses. The construction of the
proposed project would not require the use of equipment such as pile drivers, which are known to generate
substantial construction vibration levels. The primary vibration source during construction may be from a
large bulldozer. A bulldozer has a vibration impact of 0.089 inches per second peak particle velocity (PPV)
at 25 feet which is likely perceptible but below any risk of architectural damage.

The fundamental equation used to calculate vibration propagation through average soil conditions and
distance is as follows:

  PPVequipment = PPVref (25/Drec)n

  Where: PPVref = reference PPV at 25ft.
  Drec = distance from equipment to receiver in ft.
  n = 1.1 (the value related to the attenuation rate through ground)

The thresholds from the Caltrans Transportation and Construction Induced Vibration Guidance Manual
provide general thresholds and guidelines as to the vibration damage potential from vibratory impacts.

Sound Transmission Class (STC): To quantify STC, a Transmission Loss (TL) measurement is
performed in a laboratory over a range of 16 third-octave bands between 125 – 4,000 Hertz (Hz).
The average human voice creates sound within the 125 – 4,000 Hz 1/3rd octave bands.

STC is a single-number rating given to a particular material or assembly. The STC rating measures
the ability of a material or an assembly to resist airborne sound transfer over the specified
frequencies (see ASTM International Classification E413 and E90). In general, a higher STC rating
corresponds with a greater reduction of noise transmitting through a partition.

STC is highly dependent on the construction of the partition. The STC of a partition can be increased
by: adding mass, increasing or adding air space, and adding absorptive materials within the
assembly. The STC rating does not assess low-frequency sound transfer (e.g. sounds less than 125
Hz). Special consideration must be given to spaces where the noise transfer concern has lower
frequencies than speech, such as mechanical equipment and or/or music. The STC rating is a lab test
that does not take into consideration weak points, penetrations, or flanking paths.

Even with a high STC rating, any penetration, air-gap, or “flanking path can seriously degrade the
isolation quality of a wall. Flanking paths are the means for sound to transfer from one space to
another other than through the wall. Sound can flank over, under, or around a wall. Sound can also
travel through common ductwork, plumbing, or corridors. Noise will travel between spaces at the
weakest points. Typically, there is no reason to spend money or effort to improve the walls until all
weak points are controlled first.
 Outdoor Living Area: Outdoor spaces that are associated with residential land uses typically used
for passive recreational activities or other noise-sensitive uses. Such spaces include patio areas,
barbecue areas, jacuzzi areas, etc. associated with residential uses; outdoor patient recovery or
resting areas associated with hospitals, convalescent hospitals, or rest homes; outdoor areas
associated with places of worship which have a significant role in services or other noise-sensitive
activities; and outdoor school facilities routinely used for educational purposes which may be
adversely impacted by noise. Outdoor areas usually not included in this definition are: front yard
areas, driveways, greenbelts, maintenance areas and storage areas associated with residential land
uses; exterior areas at hospitals that are not used for patient activities; outdoor areas associated
with places of worship and principally used for short-term social gatherings; and, outdoor areas
associated with school facilities that are not typically associated with educational uses prone to
adverse noise impacts (for example, school play yard areas).

Percent Noise Levels: See L(n).

Sound Level (Noise Level): The weighted sound pressure level obtained by use of a sound level
meter having a standard frequency filter for attenuating part of the sound spectrum.

Sound Level Meter: An instrument, including a microphone, an amplifier, an output meter, and
frequency weighting networks for the measurement and determination of noise and sound levels.

Single Event Noise Exposure Level (SENEL): The dB(A) level which, if it lasted for one second, would
produce the same A-weighted sound energy as the actual event.

Subject:  Cumulative Analysis Beacon St – Cat32 Exemption Noise Impact Assessment – Avalon, CA

Dear Ms. Gilbert:

MD Acoustics, LLC (MD) has completed a cumulative noise impact assessment for the proposed hotel
project located at 301-305 Beacon Street in the City of Avalon, CA. The project has filed for a Categorical 32
Exemption (Cat32), which is an “Infill” Categorical Exemption (CEQA Guideline Section 15332) that exempts
infill development within urbanized areas if it meets certain criteria. The class consists of environmentally
benign infill projects that are consistent with the local General Plan and Zoning requirements. This class is
not intended for projects that would result in any significant traffic, noise, air quality, or water quality
impacts. It may apply to residential, commercial, industrial, and/or mixed-use projects.

This noise assessment intends to demonstrate the project’s compliance with applicable noise regulations
and lack of significant noise impacts. A list of definitions and terminology is located in Appendix A.

1.0  Project Description and Assessment Overview

2.0  Fundamentals of Noise
The following provides basic information about noise and presents some of the terms used within the
report.

2.1  Human Response to Changes in Noise Levels
In general, the healthy human ear is most sensitive to sounds between 1,000 Hz and 5,000 Hz (A-
weighted scale), and it perceives a sound within that range as being more intense than a sound with a
higher or lower frequency with the same magnitude. For purposes of this report, as well as with most
environmental documents, the A-scale weighting is typically reported in terms of A-weighted decibels
(dBA). Typically, the human ear can barely perceive a change in noise level of 3 dB. A change in 5 dB is
readily perceptible, and a change in 10 dB is perceived as being twice or half as loud. As previously
discussed, a doubling of sound energy results in a 3 dB increase in sound, which means that a doubling
of sound energy (e.g., doubling the volume of traffic on a highway) would result in a barely perceptible
change in sound level.

2.2  Noise Descriptors
Noise in our daily environment fluctuates over time. Some noise levels occur in regular patterns, while
others are random. Some noise levels are constant, while others are sporadic. Noise descriptors were
created to describe the different time-varying noise levels.

A-Weighted Sound Level: The sound pressure level in decibels as measured on a sound level meter using
the A-weighted filter network. The A-weighting filter de-emphasizes the very low and very high-frequency

components of the sound in a manner similar to the response of the human ear. A numerical method of
rating human judgment of loudness.

Ambient Noise Level: The composite of noise from all sources, near and far. In this context, the ambient
noise level constitutes the normal or existing level of environmental noise at a given location.

Community Noise Equivalent Level (CNEL): The average equivalent A-weighted sound level during a 24-
hour day, obtained after the addition of five (5) decibels to sound levels in the evening from 7:00 to 10:00
PM and after the addition of ten (10) decibels to sound levels in the night before 7:00 AM and after 10:00
PM.

Decibel (dB): A unit for measuring the amplitude of a sound equal to 20 times the logarithm to the base
10 of the ratio of the pressure of the sound measured to the reference pressure, which is 20 micro-pascals.

dB(A): A-weighted sound level (see definition above).

Equivalent Sound Level (LEQ): The sound level corresponding to a steady noise level over a given sample
period with the same amount of acoustic energy as the actual time-varying noise level. The energy average
noise level during the sample period.

Habitable Room: Any room meeting the requirements of the Uniform Building Code or other applicable
regulations which is intended to be used for sleeping, living, cooking, or dining purposes, excluding such
enclosed spaces as closets, pantries, bath or toilet rooms, service rooms, connecting corridors, laundries,
unfinished attics, foyers, storage spaces, cellars, utility rooms, and similar spaces.

L(n): The A-weighted sound level exceeded during a certain percentage of the sample time. For example,
L10 in the sound level exceeded 10 percent of the sample time. Similarly L50, L90 and L99, etc.

Noise: Any unwanted sound or sound that is undesirable because it interferes with speech and hearing, is
intense enough to damage hearing, or is otherwise annoying. The State Noise Control Act defines noise as
"...excessive undesirable sound...".

Outdoor Living Area: Outdoor spaces that are associated with residential land uses typically used for
passive recreational activities or other noise-sensitive uses. Such spaces include patio areas, barbecue
areas, jacuzzi areas, etc., associated with residential uses; outdoor patient recovery or resting areas
associated with hospitals, convalescent hospitals, or rest homes; outdoor areas associated with places of
worship which have a significant role in services or other noise-sensitive activities; and outdoor school
facilities routinely used for educational purposes which may be adversely impacted by noise. Outdoor
areas usually not included in this definition are: front yard areas, driveways, greenbelts, maintenance
areas, and storage areas associated with residential land uses; exterior areas at hospitals that are not used
for patient activities; outdoor areas associated with places of worship and principally used for short-term
social gatherings; and, outdoor areas associated with school facilities that are not typically associated with
educational uses prone to adverse noise impacts (for example, school play yard areas).

impacts to the adjacent land uses. SP is capable of evaluating multiple stationary noise source impacts at

equipment noise level data) to calculate noise level projections. The software allows the user to input
specific noise sources, spectral content, sound barriers, building placement, topography, and sensitive
receptor locations.

4.5  Construction Vibration Model
Construction activities can produce vibration that may be felt by adjacent land uses. The construction of the
proposed project would not require the use of equipment such as pile drivers, which are known to generate
substantial construction vibration levels. The primary vibration source during construction may be from a
large bulldozer. A bulldozer has a vibration impact of 0.089 inches per second peak particle velocity (PPV)
at 25 feet which is likely perceptible but below any risk of architectural damage.

The fundamental equation used to calculate vibration propagation through average soil conditions and
distance is as follows:

  PPVequipment = PPVref (25/Drec)n

  Where: PPVref = reference PPV at 25ft.
  Drec = distance from equipment to receiver in ft.
  n = 1.1 (the value related to the attenuation rate through ground)

The thresholds from the Caltrans Transportation and Construction Induced Vibration Guidance Manual
provide general thresholds and guidelines as to the vibration damage potential from vibratory impacts.

Room Criterion (RC) Method: When sound quality
in the space is important, the RC metric provides a
diagnostic tool to quantify both the speech
interference level and spectral imbalance.

Sound Level (Noise Level): The weighted sound
pressure level obtained by use of a sound level
meter having a standard frequency filter for
attenuating part of the sound spectrum.

Sound Level Meter: An instrument, including a
microphone, an amplifier, an output meter, and
frequency  weighting  networks  for  the
measurement and determination of noise and
sound levels.

Sound Transmission Class (STC): To quantify STC, a Transmission Loss (TL) measurement is
performed in a laboratory over a range of 16 third-octave bands between 125 – 4,000 Hertz (Hz).
The average human voice creates sound within the 125 – 4,000 Hz 1/3rd octave bands.

STC is a single-number rating given to a particular material or assembly. The STC rating measures
the ability of a material or an assembly to resist airborne sound transfer over the specified
frequencies (see ASTM International Classification E413 and E90). In general, a higher STC rating
corresponds with a greater reduction of noise transmitting through a partition.

STC is highly dependent on the construction of the partition. The STC of a partition can be increased
by: adding mass, increasing or adding air space, and adding absorptive materials within the
assembly. The STC rating does not assess low-frequency sound transfer (e.g. sounds less than 125
Hz). Special consideration must be given to spaces where the noise transfer concern has lower
frequencies than speech, such as mechanical equipment and or/or music. The STC rating is a lab test
that does not take into consideration weak points, penetrations, or flanking paths.

Even with a high STC rating, any penetration, air-gap, or “flanking path can seriously degrade the
isolation quality of a wall. Flanking paths are the means for sound to transfer from one space to
another other than through the wall. Sound can flank over, under, or around a wall. Sound can also
travel through common ductwork, plumbing, or corridors. Noise will travel between spaces at the
weakest points. Typically, there is no reason to spend money or effort to improve the walls until all
weak points are controlled first.
 Outdoor Living Area: Outdoor spaces that are associated with residential land uses typically used
for passive recreational activities or other noise-sensitive uses. Such spaces include patio areas,
barbecue areas, jacuzzi areas, etc. associated with residential uses; outdoor patient recovery or
resting areas associated with hospitals, convalescent hospitals, or rest homes; outdoor areas
associated with places of worship which have a significant role in services or other noise-sensitive
activities; and outdoor school facilities routinely used for educational purposes which may be
adversely impacted by noise. Outdoor areas usually not included in this definition are: front yard
areas, driveways, greenbelts, maintenance areas and storage areas associated with residential land
uses; exterior areas at hospitals that are not used for patient activities; outdoor areas associated
with places of worship and principally used for short-term social gatherings; and, outdoor areas
associated with school facilities that are not typically associated with educational uses prone to
adverse noise impacts (for example, school play yard areas).

Percent Noise Levels: See L(n).

Sound Level (Noise Level): The weighted sound pressure level obtained by use of a sound level
meter having a standard frequency filter for attenuating part of the sound spectrum.

Sound Level Meter: An instrument, including a microphone, an amplifier, an output meter, and
frequency weighting networks for the measurement and determination of noise and sound levels.

Single Event Noise Exposure Level (SENEL): The dB(A) level which, if it lasted for one second, would
produce the same A-weighted sound energy as the actual event.

Dear Ms. Gilbert:
MD Acoustics, LLC (MD) has completed a focused Air Quality Impact Evaluation for the proposed hotel
project located at 305 Beacon Street in the City of Avalon, CA. The purpose of this focused study is to
evaluate the air quality construction and operational emissions generated by the proposed project and to
compare the project emissions to South Coast Air Quality Management District’s (SCAQMD) thresholds of
significance as it relates to residential and commercial uses and consistency to the City’s General Plan. A
list of definitions and terminology is located in Appendix A.
1.0  Project Description
The project site is located at 305 Beacon Street within the City of Avalon, California, as shown in Exhibit A.
The site is currently zoned as Special Commercial. Land zoning surrounding the site includes Special
Commercial to the north, south, southeast, and west, and Commercial to the northeast. Metropole
Avenue is to the northwest, and Beacon Street is to the northeast.

The project proposes a two (2) story hotel with multiple uses consisting of 10 hotel rooms and a rooftop
deck for guests. The rooftop deck will include a restroom and a shallow adult-only swimming pool and is
assumed to have a maximum capacity of approximately 25 people. The rooftop operational hours will be 8
AM to 10 PM for events and rooftop amenities. See Appendix B for the architectural plans.
2.0  Thresholds of Significance
Project emissions were compared to both regional and localized SCAQMD’s thresholds of significance for
construction and operational emissions1,2.

3.0  Evaluation Procedure/Methodology
MD utilized the latest version of CalEEMod (2022.1.1.29) to calculate both the construction and
operational emissions from the project site3. Project construction is modeled to commence no earlier than
February 2026 and be completed by December 2026. Construction assumes grading, building
construction, paving, and architectural coating. Demolition will be done by hand. CalEEmod defaults were
utilized. Assumptions and output calculations are provided in Appendix C.

5.3  Cumulative Construction Impact
The Project area is out of attainment for both ozone and PM10 particulate matter. Construction of
cumulative projects will further degrade the local air quality, as well as the air quality of the South Coast
Air Basin. The greatest cumulative impact on the quality of regional air cell will be the incremental
addition of pollutants mainly from grading and architectural coating. Air quality will be temporarily
degraded during construction activities that occur separately or simultaneously. However, in accordance
with the SCAQMD methodology, projects that do not exceed the SCAQMD criteria or can be mitigated to
less than criteria levels are not significant and do not add to the overall cumulative impact. The Project
does not exceed any of the thresholds of significance and therefore is considered less than significant.

5.5  Localized Operational Emissions
Project-related air emissions from on-site sources such as architectural coatings, landscaping equipment,
on-site usage of natural gas appliances as well as the operation of vehicles on-site may have the potential
to exceed the State and Federal air quality standards in the project vicinity, even though these pollutant
emissions may not be significant enough to create a regional impact to the Air Basin. However, it should
be noted that the project would most likely not bring additional vehicle trips to the area due to the limits
on vehicles on Catalina Island. Trips would primarily be generated by taking workers and guests to and
from transportation to the island, such as a ferry, and would not occur on the island.

According to SCAQMD LST methodology, LSTs would apply to the operational phase of a project, if the
project includes stationary sources, or attracts mobile sources (such as heavy-duty trucks) that may spend
long periods queuing and idling at the site; such as industrial warehouse/transfer facilities. The proposed
project is a hotel and does not include such uses. Therefore, due to the lack of stationary source
emissions, no long-term localized significance threshold analysis is warranted.

5.6  Asbestos and Lead-Based Paint
Asbestos-containing materials (ACMs) and lead-based paint (LBP) have the potential to be present in the
existing buildings to be demolished. ACMs and lead become a health hazard once disturbed such as during
demolition activities. Long-term chronic and acute exposure to asbestos fibers may cause respiratory
diseases such as lung cancer, asbestosis and mesothelioma. When lead is absorbed into the body, it can
cause damage to the brain and other vital organs, like the kidneys, nerves, and blood.

The Project would be required to comply with the requirements of SCAQMD Rule 1403 regarding the
abatement and disposal of ACMs and LBP found during construction activities. Rule 1403 regulates
asbestos and lead as toxic materials and controls the emissions of asbestos and lead from demolition and
renovation activities by specifying agency notifications, appropriate removal procedures, and handling and
clean‐up procedures. Rule 1403 applies to owners and operators involved in the demolition or renovation
of ACM- and LBP-containing structures, storage facilities, and waste disposal sites. The requirements
under Rule 1403 include: surveying structures for ACM and LBP; agency notification of intention to
remove asbestos and lead; ACM and LBP removal procedures and time schedules; ACM and LBP handling
and clean‐up procedures; ACM and LBP storage, disposal, and landfill requirements; and record keeping.
In addition, any facility known to contain asbestos or lead is required to have a written management plan

Temperature and Extreme Heat data are for grid cell in which your project are located. The projection is based on the 98th historical percentile of daily maximum/minimum temperatures from
observed historical data (32 climate model ensemble from Cal-Adapt, 2040–2059 average under RCP 8.5). Each grid cell is 6 kilometers (km) by 6 km, or 3.7 miles (mi) by 3.7 mi.
Extreme Precipitation data are for the grid cell in which your project are located. The threshold of 20 mm is equivalent to about ¾ an inch of rain, which would be light to moderate rainfall if

Sea Level Rise data are for the grid cell in which your project are located. The projections are from Radke et al. (2017), as reported in Cal-Adapt (Radke et al., 2017, CEC-500-2017-008), and
consider inundation location and depth for the San Francisco Bay, the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta and California coast resulting different increments of sea level rise coupled with
extreme storm events. Users may select from four scenarios to view the range in potential inundation depth for the grid cell. The four scenarios are: No rise, 0.5 meter, 1.0 meter, 1.41 meters
Wildfire data are for the grid cell in which your project are located. The projections are from UC Davis, as reported in Cal-Adapt (2040–2059 average under RCP 8.5), and consider historical data
of climate, vegetation, population density, and large (> 400 ha) fire history. Users may select from four model simulations to view the range in potential wildfire probabilities for the grid cell. The
four simulations make different assumptions about expected rainfall and temperature are: Warmer/drier (HadGEM2-ES), Cooler/wetter (CNRM-CM5), Average conditions (CanESM2), Range of
different rainfall and temperature possibilities (MIROC5). Each grid cell is 6 kilometers (km) by 6 km, or 3.7 miles (mi) by 3.7 mi.
